messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Community Organizer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Darkness: Dark spaces, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kareem, a 54-year-old Middle Eastern American community organizer, came to treatment after years of trying to keep himself moving through work, family life, and public meetings while never quite feeling safe in his own skin. The assault that changed him had happened in the apartment he shared with his then partner, a man he had trusted completely. What began as an argument in a dark hallway escalated into physical abuse that left Kareem pinned, frightened, and unable to make sense of where one moment ended and the next began. Even now, his memories of that night returned in disconnected pieces: the smell of the apartment, a hand grabbing his arm, the pounding in his ears, the flash of a wall, and, most intrusively, fragments of sounds he had heard during the attack. When he was overtaken by those memories, he sometimes heard those same sounds in his head as if they were happening again, and the recollection could be brought on instantly by something in his surroundings without warning. A dim corridor, a shadowed stairwell, or the sound of a helicopter or low-flying aircraft over the neighborhood could pull him back before he had time to prepare.

From the beginning, Kareem made sense of the event through a painful set of conclusions about himself and other people. He said he had been betrayed by someone he trusted, and that betrayal seemed to confirm for him that the world no longer worked the way he had believed it did. He spoke with shame about the thought that the abuse happened because of the sort of person he was, as if there were something about him that invited mistreatment. Those beliefs did not stay abstract; they colored the memories themselves. When an image of the attack surfaced, it came attached to self-condemnation and to the conviction that trust was foolish, so the memory felt not only vivid but morally loaded, as if each fragment proved that he had misjudged both his partner and himself. Over time, the same remembered pieces deepened his sense that everything he once relied on had been destroyed.

Kareem’s attempts to cope slowly hardened into habits that shaped his days. He became vigilant for dangerous people, scanning faces in crowds, watching hands, and checking exits whenever he entered a meeting hall, parking garage, or public building. He avoided the site where the assault had taken place, taking longer routes home and declining invitations that would bring him near that street. He also began wearing concealing clothing, favoring loose layers and darker jackets that helped him feel less visible, as though being harder to notice might keep him from becoming a target again. These strategies briefly lowered his alarm, but they also kept his fear alive. Because he was constantly watching for threat, ordinary movement in a doorway, a stranger standing too close, or a sudden shadow in a hallway became more likely to catch his attention, and each new jolt could unexpectedly call up the old memory. In that way, the very effort to protect himself made the world feel full of possible dangers and made his trigger list grow broader.

The more often the memories broke through, the more Kareem returned to the same explanations. Each intruding fragment seemed to confirm that he was marked by what had happened, that he had failed to read the danger correctly, and that the world could no longer be trusted. Those appraisals intensified his sense of threat, and his scanning became more relentless. At work, in his role as a community organizer, he found himself preoccupied with who might be unsafe in the room, while the dark basement meeting spaces and windowless offices he sometimes had to use became especially hard to tolerate. He began arriving early to choose seats, leaving before others, and turning down evening events that would have kept him out after sunset. The concealing clothing and avoidance of the old site protected him from brief spikes of panic, but they also narrowed his life and reinforced the belief that danger was everywhere and that he himself was somehow the reason it had found him.

By the time Kareem sought help, he was exhausted by the loop of being set off, reliving the assault in fragments and sounds, and then retreating further into suspicion and self-blame. He feared that one unguarded moment in the dark, one unexpected aircraft overhead, or one accidental return to that neighborhood could bring the whole memory crashing back again. What brought him in was the sense that he could no longer keep organizing for his community while living as if every room might contain harm, and what he most hoped for was to stop feeling betrayed by the world and by himself long enough to trust his own life again.
